Content:
Suppose we conduct a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a population of size [MATH: N] where some proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable [MATH: X_i] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: {1, [math]i[/math]th member of the sample has the characteristic; 0, otherwise]

Content:
In other words,

Content:
[MATH: X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).]

Content:
Let's assume the sample size is less than (or equal to) [MATH: 5\%] of the population size. Under this condition, we've seen that [MATH: X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n] can be considered to be (approximately) independent and identically distributed, which means that

Content:
[MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p),]

Content:
where [MATH: B(n,p)] denotes a binomial distribution, and

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).]

Content:
Remember that [MATH: X] represents the number of sample members with the characteristic.

Content:
Now, let's assume that [MATH: np > 5] and [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] so we can apply the normal approximation of the binomial distribution (i.e., the central limit theorem). Then,

Content:
[MATH: X \approx N\big(np,np(1-p)\big).]

Content:
Furthermore, we've also seen that we can construct an estimator [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] as

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} = \dfrac{X}{n}]

Content:
where

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: X] is approximately normally distributed, [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] is also normally distributed. Therefore, the sampling distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p}\approx N\bigg(p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\bigg).]

Content:
Finally, since we usually don't know [MATH: p,] we can use a particular estimate to approximate [MATH: \textrm{E}[{\widehat{\,p}}]] and [MATH: \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}].]

Content:

sections.normalized_html:
Given a population in which a proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] can be approximated as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \right),]

where

  • [MATH: n\leq 5\% \cdot N] (the sample size is less than (or equal to) [MATH: 5\%] of the population size),

  • [MATH: np > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements have the characteristic), and

  • [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements do not have the characteristic).

Let's now examine each situation.

  • In situation I, we have [MATH: n|= 120; ≤ 5% ⋅ N; = 0.05 ⋅ 20000; = 1000✓; np|= 120(0.75); = 90; > 5✓; n(1 − p)|= 120(1 − 0.75); = 30; > 5.✓] Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] using the given model.

  • In situation II, we have [MATH: n|= 25,; 5% ⋅ N|= 0.05 ⋅ 200; = 10; < 25.×] Since the sample size is more than [MATH: 5\%] of the population size, we cannot approximate the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] using the given model.

  • In situation III, we're given that the population is significantly larger than the sample size in each case. Therefore, we may assume that the first condition is satisfied.

    For the other conditions, we have [MATH: np|= 45(0.9); = 40.5; > 5✓; n(1 − p)|= 45(1 − 0.9); = 4.5; ≯5.×] Since [MATH: n(1-p) \ngtr 5,] we cannot approximate the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] using the given model.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we conduct a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a population of size [MATH: N] where some proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable [MATH: X_i] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: {1, [math]i[/math]th member of the sample has the characteristic; 0, otherwise]

Content:
In other words,

Content:
[MATH: X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).]

Content:
Let's assume the sample size is less than (or equal to) [MATH: 5\%] of the population size. Under this condition, we've seen that [MATH: X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n] can be considered to be (approximately) independent and identically distributed, which means that

Content:
[MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p),]

Content:
where [MATH: B(n,p)] denotes a binomial distribution, and

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).]

Content:
Remember that [MATH: X] represents the number of sample members with the characteristic.

Content:
Now, let's assume that [MATH: np > 5] and [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] so we can apply the normal approximation of the binomial distribution (i.e., the central limit theorem). Then,

Content:
[MATH: X \approx N\big(np,np(1-p)\big).]

Content:
Furthermore, we've also seen that we can construct an estimator [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] as

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} = \dfrac{X}{n}]

Content:
where

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: X] is approximately normally distributed, [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] is also normally distributed. Therefore, the sampling distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p}\approx N\bigg(p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\bigg).]

Content:
Finally, since we usually don't know [MATH: p,] we can use a particular estimate to approximate [MATH: \textrm{E}[{\widehat{\,p}}]] and [MATH: \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}].]

Content:
Watch out! In this lesson, [MATH: N] denotes the size of a population, while [MATH: N(\cdot,\cdot)] denotes the normal distribution.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Summary of the Sample Distribution Model

Content:
Let's summarize everything we know about the sampling distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
> Suppose we have a population of size [MATH: N] in which a proportion [MATH: p] has a particular characteristic. Consider a sample of size [MATH: n] drawn from the population, where
>
> - [MATH: n \leq 5\%\cdot N] (the sample size is smaller than (or equal to) [MATH: 5\%] of the population size),
> - [MATH: np > 5,] and
> - [MATH: n(1-p) > 5].
>
> Then, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] can be approximated as the normally distributed random variable [MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \right).]

Content:
The flow chart below summarizes the steps that led us to this model.

Content:
Finally, note that the conditions [MATH: np > 5] and [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] have a particular interpretation in this context:

Content:
- [MATH: np > 5] means the expected number of sample members with the characteristic is greater than [MATH: 5,]
- [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] means the expected number of sample members without the characteristic is greater than [MATH: 5.]

Item 3 — Example: Identifying Situations When the CLT for Proportions is Appropriate

Example Prompt:
For which of the following situations can the distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] be approximated as
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left(p,\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\right),]
where [MATH: p] is the population proportion?

1. A sample of [MATH: 120] apricots from a population of [MATH: 20\,000], where [MATH: 75\%] of the apricots weigh more than [MATH: 50] g.
2. A sample of [MATH: 25] gym members from a population containing [MATH: 200] members, where [MATH: 80\%] of the gym's members work out for more than [MATH: 100] minutes each visit.
3. A sample of [MATH: 45] flights in an airport, given that [MATH: 90\%] of flights arrive on time. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Given a population in which a proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] can be approximated as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \right),]

where

- [MATH: n\leq 5\% \cdot N] (the sample size is less than (or equal to) [MATH: 5\%] of the population size),
- [MATH: np > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements have the characteristic), and
- [MATH: n(1-p) > 5] (more than [MATH: 5] sample elements do not have the characteristic).

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have
[MATH: n|= 120; ≤ 5% ⋅ N; = 0.05 ⋅ 20000; = 1000✓; np|= 120(0.75); = 90; > 5✓; n(1 − p)|= 120(1 − 0.75); = 30; > 5.✓]
Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] using the given model.
- In situation II, we have
[MATH: n|= 25,; 5% ⋅ N|= 0.05 ⋅ 200; = 10; < 25.×]
Since the sample size is more than [MATH: 5\%] of the population size, we cannot approximate the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] using the given model.
- In situation III, we're given that the population is significantly larger than the sample size in each case. Therefore, we may assume that the first condition is satisfied.

For the other conditions, we have
[MATH: np|= 45(0.9); = 40.5; > 5✓; n(1 − p)|= 45(1 − 0.9); = 4.5; ≯5.×]
Since [MATH: n(1-p) \ngtr 5,] we cannot approximate the distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] using the given model.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \right),]

[MATH: P(\widehat{\,p} > 0.5).]

[MATH: P(p^(^) > 0.5)|= P(Z > (0.5 − 0.42)/(sqrt(0.0029))); ≈ P(Z > 1.49); = 1 − P(Z < 1.49); = 1 − Φ(1.49).]
